answer: Any five of: never put sharp objects in the ear; clean only the outer ear with a damp cloth; avoid very loud noise and loud earphones; treat infections early; do not slap anyone on the ear; protect ears from cold; go for check-ups.

subject: Science
question: Name the three types of musical instruments and give one example of each.
answer: String — guitar or adungu; wind — flute or whistle; percussion — drum or xylophone.

subject: Science
question: Name the three parts of the circulatory system.
answer: The heart, the blood vessels and the blood.

subject: Science
question: Where is the heart found, and what protects it?
answer: In the chest, slightly to the left, protected by the ribs (and the breastbone).

subject: Science
question: Name the four chambers of the heart and state the work of each.
answer: Right atrium — receives blood without oxygen from the body; right ventricle — pumps it to the lungs; left atrium — receives blood with oxygen from the lungs; left ventricle — pumps it to the whole body.

subject: Science
question: Why does the left ventricle have the thickest wall?
answer: Because it pumps blood to the whole body, which needs much greater force than pumping to the lungs.

subject: Science
question: What is the work of the valves in the heart?
answer: They stop blood from flowing backwards.

subject: Science
question: Name the three types of blood vessels and give one difference between arteries and veins.
answer: Arteries, veins and capillaries. Arteries carry blood away from the heart with thick elastic walls at high pressure, while veins carry blood back to the heart, have thinner walls and contain valves.

subject: Science
question: Which artery carries blood without oxygen, and which vein carries blood with oxygen?
answer: The pulmonary artery carries blood without oxygen; the pulmonary vein carries blood with oxygen.

subject: Science
question: Name the four parts of blood and give the work of each.
answer: Plasma — carries food, water, salts and waste; red blood cells — carry oxygen; white blood cells — fight germs; platelets — help the blood to clot.

subject: Science
question: Name the four blood groups.
answer: A, B, AB and O.

subject: Science
question: Give any four functions of blood.
answer: Any four of: transporting oxygen; transporting food and water; carrying waste to the excretory organs; fighting germs; clotting to stop bleeding; spreading heat round the body.

subject: Science
question: Name any four diseases or disorders of the circulatory system.
answer: Any four of: anaemia, sickle cell disease, leukaemia, high blood pressure, heart attack, haemophilia, varicose veins.

subject: Science
question: Give three ways in which HIV can be spread through blood, and three ways of preventing this.
answer: Spread: transfusion of untested blood; sharing needles or syringes; sharing razor blades or other skin-cutting instruments (also mother to child). Prevention: use only screened blood; use sterile single-use needles; never share razor blades or sharp instruments (and mothers who are HIV positive should follow medical advice).

subject: Science
question: Give any five ways of increasing the volume of blood in the body.
answer: Any five of: eat iron-rich foods such as dodo, nakati, liver, beans and meat; eat fruits rich in vitamin C; deworm regularly; sleep under a mosquito net; treat wounds and bleeding quickly; exercise; rest well; have a transfusion of screened blood in serious cases.

subject: Science
question: Why should blood for transfusion be tested first?
answer: To make sure it is the right blood group for the patient and that it is free from germs and infections such as HIV, hepatitis and syphilis, so that the transfusion helps instead of harming.

subject: Science
question: Trace the path of blood from the body back to the body, naming the chambers and the lungs.
answer: Body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs (to get oxygen) → left atrium → left ventricle → back to the body.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: What is alcoholism? Who is an alcoholic?
answer: Alcoholism is the condition of being unable to stop taking alcohol — addiction to alcohol. An alcoholic is a person who is addicted to alcohol.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Give any four effects of alcoholism on the individual.
answer: Any four of: damage to the liver, stomach and brain; loss of memory and poor judgement; accidents and injuries; loss of job and poverty; poor health, malnutrition and early death.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Give any three effects of alcoholism on the family and three on the community.
answer: Family: money wasted instead of buying food and paying fees; quarrels and violence; children dropping out of school; neglect of the family. Community: crime and insecurity; road accidents; loss of a productive workforce; extra burden on hospitals and police. (Any three each.)

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Name any three harmful substances found in tobacco smoke and what each does.
answer: Nicotine — causes addiction; tar — causes cancer; carbon monoxide — reduces the oxygen carried by the blood.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Give the difference between active and passive smoking.
answer: Active smoking is smoking a cigarette yourself; passive smoking is breathing in the smoke of somebody else who is smoking.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Why is passive smoking dangerous, especially for children and pregnant mothers?
answer: Because passive smokers breathe the same harmful substances and suffer the same diseases, and children's lungs and unborn babies are still developing, so the harm is greater — it can cause coughs, chest infections, poor growth and low birth weight.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Give any four effects of smoking on a person's health.
answer: Any four of: lung cancer; chronic cough and bronchitis; tuberculosis; heart disease; stained teeth and bad breath; poor appetite; addiction.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: What are essential drugs? Give any four examples.
answer: Essential drugs are the medicines a community most needs and which should always be available at a health centre. Examples: ORS, paracetamol, anti-malarial tablets, antibiotics, deworming tablets, vaccines (any four).

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Give any four characteristics of good drugs.
answer: Any four of: within the expiry date; properly sealed and labelled; from a licensed health centre or pharmacy; with the correct name, dose and instructions; not discoloured, crushed or damp.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Give any five rules for storing drugs safely in a home.
answer: Any five of: keep them in a cool, dry, dark place; keep them in the original labelled container; close them tightly; keep them out of reach of children, preferably locked; do not store them with food or paraffin; check the expiry date; destroy or return expired drugs safely.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Give the difference between drug abuse and drug misuse, with one example of each.
answer: Drug abuse is using a drug for a purpose it was not meant for, for example sniffing petrol. Drug misuse is using a proper medicine wrongly, for example taking the wrong dose or using somebody else's prescription.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: What is drug dependence?
answer: Drug dependence is when the body or the mind can no longer do without the drug, so the person suffers when he or she stops taking it.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Name any four commonly abused substances.
answer: Any four of: alcohol, tobacco, marijuana (njaga), khat (mairungi), petrol or glue fumes, cocaine, heroin, wrongly used sleeping tablets.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Give any five factors that lead young people into alcoholism, smoking or drug abuse.
answer: Any five of: peer pressure; curiosity; idleness and too much free time; copying parents or film and music stars; advertising; frustration and family problems; easy availability; lack of guidance.

subject: Science
topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
question: Name any five life skills that help a young person to refuse drugs, and explain one of them.
answer: Any five of: assertiveness, peer pressure resistance, decision-making, critical thinking, self-esteem, coping with stress, effective communication, using free time well. Assertiveness, for example, is the ability to say NO firmly and to repeat it without fear or apology, and to walk away from the situation.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between flowering and non-flowering plants, with two examples of each.
answer: Flowering plants produce flowers and seeds, for example maize and mango; non-flowering plants do not produce flowers, for example ferns and pine.

subject: Science
question: Name the three groups of non-flowering plants and give one example of each.
answer: Spore-bearing plants — fern; conifers — pine; algae — spirogyra (or seaweed).

subject: Science
question: Give three differences between legumes and cereals.
answer: Legumes: seeds in pods, two seed leaves, root nodules that add nitrogen, rich in protein. Cereals: grasses grown for grain, one seed leaf, fibrous roots, rich in carbohydrates. (Any three pairs.)

subject: Science
question: Why is planting legumes good for the soil?
answer: Because their root nodules contain bacteria that add nitrogen to the soil, making it fertile again for the next crop.

subject: Science
question: Name the male and the female parts of a flower and state the work of each.
answer: The stamen (anther and filament) is the male part and makes pollen; the pistil (stigma, style and ovary) is the female part and receives pollen and holds the ovules.

subject: Science
question: What is pollination, and what happens to the ovary after fertilisation?
answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma. After fertilisation the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovules become seeds.

subject: Science
question: What is seed dispersal, and give any four reasons why it is necessary?
answer: Seed dispersal is the scattering of seeds away from the parent plant. Reasons: to avoid overcrowding; to reduce competition for water, light and food; to spread the plant to new areas; to reduce the spread of pests and diseases (any four).

subject: Science
question: Name the five agents of seed dispersal.
answer: Wind, water, animals (and birds), explosive mechanism, and people.

subject: Science
question: Give the features of a seed dispersed by wind and one dispersed by animals.
answer: Wind: the seed is light and has wings, hairs or a parachute. Animals: the fruit is sweet and fleshy so it is eaten, or the seed has hooks that stick to fur and clothes.

subject: Science
question: What is plant propagation? Name its two types.
answer: Plant propagation is the way new plants are produced from old ones. Its two types are sexual (by seeds) and vegetative (asexual).

subject: Science
question: Name any six methods of vegetative propagation, with one example of each.
answer: Any six: cuttings — cassava; suckers — banana; tubers — Irish potato; bulbs — onion; rhizomes — ginger; runners — grass; grafting — mango; layering — guava.

subject: Science
question: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
answer: Advantages: the new plant is exactly like the parent and it matures faster. Disadvantages: diseases are passed on easily and there is no variety among the plants.

subject: Science
question: Give any six economic values of plants.
answer: Any six of: food; cash crops and employment; timber and poles; firewood and charcoal; medicine; raw materials for industries; fodder for animals; shade and windbreaks; protection of the environment and supply of oxygen; tourism.

subject: Science
question: Why do farmers plant beans in a garden where maize was grown the season before?
answer: Because the beans are a legume whose root nodules add nitrogen to the soil, restoring the fertility that the maize used up. This is crop rotation.

subject: Science
question: Give one plant grown from each of: cuttings, suckers, bulbs, rhizomes, tubers.
answer: Cuttings — cassava; suckers — banana; bulbs — onion; rhizomes — ginger; tubers — Irish potato (or sweet potato).

subject: Science
question: Name the four types of cattle and what each is kept for.
answer: Dairy — milk; beef — meat; dual-purpose — both milk and meat; work (draught) — ploughing and pulling carts.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between indigenous and exotic breeds, with two examples of each.
answer: Indigenous breeds have always been in the country, for example Ankole long-horned and Zebu; exotic breeds were brought from other countries, for example Friesian and Jersey.

subject: Science
question: Give two advantages of indigenous breeds and two of exotic breeds.
answer: Indigenous: resist diseases and heat, and can walk long distances for pasture and water. Exotic: give much more milk or meat, and mature faster.

subject: Science
question: Name any six external features of a cow.
answer: Any six of: horns, eyes, ears, muzzle, dewlap, hump, udder with teats, tail, hooves, hide, back, flank.

subject: Science
question: Give three differences between a cow and a bull.
answer: A cow has an udder with four teats while a bull has none; a bull has a larger head and thicker neck and shoulders; a bull is usually stronger and fiercer, while the cow is gentler and produces milk.

subject: Science
question: Define: heifer, steer, calf.
answer: Heifer — a young female that has not yet calved; steer (ox) — a castrated male; calf — the young one of cattle.

subject: Science
question: Name any four methods of grazing cattle.
answer: Any four of: free range, paddocking, tethering, zero grazing, strip grazing.

subject: Science
question: Give three advantages of zero grazing.
answer: Any three of: it suits a small piece of land; the milk and the animal stay clean; manure is easily collected; the animal uses less energy so it gives more milk; it is easy to control diseases and feeding.

subject: Science
question: Name any five feeds given to cattle.
answer: Any five of: pasture grasses, fodder such as elephant grass, legumes such as calliandra, crop residues, concentrates such as dairy meal, mineral salt licks, and clean water.

subject: Science
question: Give any five qualities of a good cattle shed.
answer: Any five of: spacious, dry, well ventilated, easy to clean, with a concrete or sloping floor, a good roof, feeding and watering places, a calf pen, a milking area and a crush.

subject: Science
question: What is the gestation period of a cow? What is calving?
answer: The gestation period is about nine months (280 days). Calving is the act of giving birth to a calf.

subject: Science
question: What is colostrum, and why must the calf get it?
answer: Colostrum is the first thick yellow milk produced after calving. The calf must get it because it is rich in antibodies that protect it from disease, and in nutrients for a good start.

subject: Science
question: Give any three advantages of artificial insemination.
answer: Any three of: a farmer can use a very good bull without keeping one; it prevents diseases spread by mating; one bull can serve very many cows; it improves the breed quickly; it is cheaper than keeping a bull.

subject: Science
question: Give any six rules of clean milking.
answer: Any six of: milk at the same time daily; wash hands and the udder with clean warm water and dry them; use clean dry metal containers; use the full-hand method; milk quickly and completely; keep the shed clean; sieve and cool the milk at once; a sick person or sick cow must not supply milk.

subject: Science
question: Name any five milk products.
answer: Any five of: ghee, butter, yoghurt, cheese, sour milk, cream, powdered milk, ice cream.

subject: Science
question: Name any four cattle pests and the harm each causes.
answer: Any four: ticks — suck blood and spread East Coast fever; tsetse flies — spread nagana; worms — cause anaemia and poor growth; lice and mites — cause irritation and wounds.

subject: Science
question: Name any four cattle diseases and one way of controlling each.
answer: Any four, for example: foot and mouth disease — vaccination and quarantine; East Coast fever — spraying or dipping against ticks; nagana — control tsetse flies and clear bush; mastitis — clean milking and treatment; anthrax — vaccination and never opening the carcass.

subject: Science
question: Give any five practices that harm cattle.
answer: Any five of: beating and overworking; rough or over-milking; tethering with no shade or water; overstocking and overgrazing; using dirty instruments for dehorning or castration; burning pasture; using wrong or expired drugs.

subject: Science
question: Give any six steps in starting a livestock farm.
answer: Any six of: choose a suitable site; decide the type of cattle and the system; get capital and plan; prepare land, pasture and fencing; build the shed and crush; buy healthy stock; arrange feeds and water; register with the veterinary officer; keep records; find a market.

subject: Science
question: Why should a farmer keep records on a cattle farm?
answer: Because records show which cows produce most milk, when each was served and is due to calve, what treatment was given, and how much money came in and went out — so the farmer can plan, breed better animals and know whether the farm is making a profit.

subject: Science
question: What is a resource? Give three living and three non-living resources.
answer: A resource is anything in the environment that people use to satisfy their needs. Living: plants, animals, fish (also birds, insects, people). Non-living: soil, water, air (also minerals, sunlight, rocks).

subject: Science
question: Why are human beings called a resource?
answer: Because people provide labour, skills, ideas and leadership that are needed to use all the other resources and to develop the country.

subject: Science
question: What is harvesting? Give the way each of these is harvested: fish, timber, salt, minerals.
answer: Harvesting is collecting a resource from the environment for use. Fish — nets, hooks and traps; timber — felling trees and sawing; salt — evaporating water from salt lakes such as Katwe; minerals — mining, quarrying, drilling or panning.

subject: Science
question: Give any five good harvesting practices.
answer: Any five of: take only what is needed; use the right tools and methods; leave young plants, fish and animals to grow; avoid poison, explosives and undersized nets; replant after cutting trees; avoid harvesting in the breeding season; store the harvest well.

subject: Science
question: Give any four uses of water and four uses of soil.
answer: Water: drinking, cooking and washing, irrigation, fishing, transport, hydro-electric power (any four). Soil: growing crops, making bricks, making pots, building, holding plant roots (any four).

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between renewable and non-renewable resources.
answer: Renewable resources can be replaced or never run out, such as sunlight and wind; non-renewable resources get used up and cannot be replaced, such as gold and petroleum.

subject: Science
question: Classify these as renewable or non-renewable: sunlight, copper, wind, petroleum, forests.
answer: Renewable: sunlight, wind, forests. Non-renewable: copper, petroleum.

subject: Science
question: Why are plants and animals renewable only under certain conditions?
answer: Because they can only replace themselves if they are given time and conditions to reproduce. If people cut trees or catch fish faster than they can reproduce, they are used up completely and may become extinct.

subject: Science
question: What is meant by depletion of a resource? Give one example.
answer: Depletion is using up a resource until very little is left, for example over-fishing on a lake until the fish stocks nearly disappear (or over-cutting of forests).

subject: Science
question: What does it mean when an animal species is said to be extinct?
answer: It means the species no longer exists anywhere — every member of it has died and it can never be brought back.

subject: Science
question: What is conservation?
answer: Conservation is protecting and using resources carefully so that they are not destroyed or used up.

subject: Science
question: Give any five ways of conserving soil.
answer: Any five of: mulching, terracing, contour ploughing, crop rotation, applying manure, planting cover crops, controlled grazing, planting trees.

subject: Science
question: Give any four ways of conserving water.
answer: Any four of: harvesting rain water, protecting springs and wetlands, avoiding pollution, closing taps, careful irrigation, repairing leaking pipes.

subject: Science
question: Give any four ways of conserving forests and four ways of protecting wild animals and fish.
answer: Forests: afforestation, reafforestation, agroforestry, energy-saving stoves, forest reserves (any four). Animals and fish: game parks and sanctuaries, laws against poaching, closed fishing seasons, correct net sizes, fish farming (any four).

subject: Science
question: Give any five reasons why resources must be conserved.
answer: Any five of: so that resources last for future generations; to keep the environment healthy; to keep soil fertile and rainfall reliable; to protect wildlife and tourism; to avoid famine and poverty; to prevent conflicts over scarce resources.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between breathing and respiration.
answer: Breathing is simply taking in and giving out air, while respiration is the process by which the body breaks down food to release energy inside the cells.

subject: Science
question: Name any six organs of the respiratory system.
answer: Any six of: nose, pharynx, epiglottis, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, lungs, diaphragm.

subject: Science
question: State the work of: the nose, the epiglottis, the trachea, the alveoli, the diaphragm.
answer: Nose — takes in air and filters, warms and moistens it; epiglottis — closes the windpipe when swallowing; trachea — carries air to the lungs; alveoli — where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves; diaphragm — the muscle that flattens and relaxes to help breathing.

subject: Science
question: Trace the path taken by air from outside the body to the blood.
answer: Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli → blood.

subject: Science
question: Why is it better to breathe through the nose than through the mouth?
answer: Because the nose has hairs and mucus that trap dust and germs, and it warms and moistens the air before it reaches the lungs; the mouth does none of these.

subject: Science
question: Describe what happens to the diaphragm and the ribs when a person breathes in.
answer: The diaphragm flattens and moves downwards, the ribs move upwards and outwards, the chest cavity increases in size and air rushes into the lungs.

subject: Science
question: Give three differences between inhaled and exhaled air.
answer: Any three of: inhaled air has more oxygen (21% against 16%); exhaled air has much more carbon dioxide (about 4% against 0.03%); exhaled air has more water vapour; exhaled air is warmer.

subject: Science
question: Describe one experiment that shows exhaled air contains carbon dioxide.
answer: Breathe out through a straw into lime water. The lime water turns milky, showing that carbon dioxide is present. (Comparing with air blown in by a pump shows the difference.)

subject: Science
question: Describe one experiment that shows exhaled air contains water vapour.
answer: Breathe onto a cold mirror or glass. Tiny drops of water form on it, showing that exhaled air contains water vapour.

subject: Science
question: Write the word equation for respiration.
answer: Food (glucose) + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water

subject: Science
question: Give any four uses of the energy released during respiration.
answer: Any four of: movement and work; growth and repair of the body; keeping the body warm; the beating of the heart and the working of other organs; thinking; digestion.

subject: Science
question: Name any five diseases of the respiratory system.
answer: Any five of: tuberculosis, pneumonia, bronchitis, asthma, the common cold and flu, whooping cough, lung cancer, diphtheria.

subject: Science
question: Give the cause and two signs of tuberculosis.
answer: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria spread through coughing and sneezing by an infected person. Signs: a cough lasting more than two weeks, chest pain, weight loss, night sweats, fever (any two).

subject: Science
question: Give any six ways of keeping the respiratory system healthy.
answer: Any six of: do not smoke and avoid other people's smoke; keep rooms well ventilated; avoid dust and cooking smoke; cover the mouth when coughing; immunise children; eat a balanced diet; exercise regularly; breathe through the nose; avoid overcrowded rooms; treat coughs and colds early; plant trees.

subject: Science
question: How does the circulatory system help the respiratory system?
answer: The blood, especially the red blood cells, carries oxygen from the alveoli to every cell of the body, and carries the waste carbon dioxide back to the lungs to be breathed out. Without the circulatory system, the oxygen would never reach the cells.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Give the difference between clean water and safe water.
answer: Clean water has no dirt that you can see, while safe water is free from germs and harmful substances and can be drunk without causing disease. Water can look clean and still be unsafe.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Name any five impurities found in water and where each comes from.
answer: Any five, for example: human wastes — from poor latrines and open defecation; animal wastes — from animals at the water source; fertilisers and pesticides — from gardens; oils and chemicals — from factories and garages; silt and leaves — washed in by rain; rubbish and polythene — from homes.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Name any four diseases caused by drinking unsafe water.
answer: Any four of: cholera, typhoid, dysentery, diarrhoea, bilharzia, worms, hepatitis.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Name five methods of making water safe for drinking.
answer: Boiling, filtering, treating with chemicals, distilling and decanting (also solar disinfection).

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Describe how water is made safe by decanting.
answer: The dirty water is left to stand undisturbed in a container until the heavy particles settle at the bottom. The clear water on top is then poured off carefully into another clean container, leaving the sediment behind.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Why is boiling the commonest method used in homes?
answer: Because it is cheap and easy — every home has a fire — and it kills the germs that cause disease, needing no special chemicals or equipment.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Which method gives the purest water, and why?
answer: Distillation, because boiling turns the water into steam, leaving germs, salts and other dissolved substances behind; the steam is then cooled back into very pure water.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Give the correct order of treating very dirty water and say why that order is used.
answer: First decant or filter to remove the dirt you can see, then boil or treat to kill the germs, then store in a clean covered container. Filtering first is important because dirt and solid matter can protect germs from the treatment and make chemicals less effective.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Give any four rules for storing drinking water safely.
answer: Any four of: use a clean covered container; use a tap or long-handled cup so hands do not enter; never mix treated with untreated water; clean the container regularly; keep it away from animals and small children.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Give any five ways of protecting a water source.
answer: Any five of: fence the source; build a drainage channel; keep latrines at least 30 m away and downhill; do not wash clothes or bathe at the source; do not water animals there; do not dig or farm next to it; plant grass around it.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Name any four plant materials used to make salt.
answer: Any four of: dry banana peelings, banana stems, bean stalks, millet stalks, papyrus reeds, water-lily plants.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Describe, in steps, how salt is made from plant materials.
answer: Dry the plant material → burn it into ash → put the ash in a container or funnel-shaped basket lined with grass → pour clean water slowly through the ash (leaching) → collect the filtrate → boil it until all the water evaporates → the solid salt is left behind.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Which three science processes are shown when making salt from plants?
answer: Dissolving, filtering and evaporation.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Give any six steps followed when washing clothes at home.
answer: Any six of: sort the clothes; empty the pockets and shake off dust; soak them in soapy water; wash by rubbing or brushing the dirty parts; rinse two or three times; hang them in the sun to dry; iron them; fold and store them cleanly.

subject: Science
topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
question: Give any four reasons why clothes should be washed and ironed.
answer: Any four of: to remove dirt, sweat and bad smell; to kill germs and prevent skin diseases; to kill jiggers and lice by ironing; to make the clothes last longer; to look smart and keep self-respect.

subject: Science
question: What is first aid, and who is a first aider?
answer: First aid is the immediate help given to an injured or suddenly sick person before a health worker arrives or before the person reaches hospital. A first aider is the person who gives it.

subject: Science
question: Give any four aims of first aid.
answer: Any four of: to save life; to prevent the injury from getting worse; to relieve pain; to promote recovery; to get the person quickly to proper medical care.

subject: Science
question: Give any five qualities of a good first aider.
answer: Any five of: calm and confident; quick but careful; clean; kind and comforting; observant; knows his or her limits; sends for help early.

subject: Science
question: Name any eight items found in a first-aid kit.
answer: Any eight of: cotton wool, bandages, gauze, plaster, scissors, antiseptic, gloves, a thermometer, safety pins, clean water, a torch, ORS, a splint, a notebook and pen.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between a burn and a scald, with one cause of each.
answer: A burn is caused by dry heat, for example fire or a hot iron; a scald is caused by moist heat, for example hot water or steam.

subject: Science
question: Give the steps of first aid for a burn.
answer: Remove the person from the source of heat (switching off electricity if needed) → cool the part with clean cool water for 10–20 minutes → remove tight clothing near the burn before swelling → cover with a clean dry non-fluffy cloth → give fluids if the person is fully awake → take them to a health centre if the burn is large, deep or on the face or hands.

subject: Science
question: Name any four things that should never be put on a burn.
answer: Any four of: cow dung, engine oil, paraffin, mud, butter, toothpaste, ash, ice.

subject: Science
question: Give any four ways of preventing burns and scalds at home.
answer: Any four of: keep children away from the fireplace and kitchen; turn saucepan handles inwards; put out fires properly; lock away paraffin, petrol and matches; do not overload sockets; put out candles before sleeping; keep hot drinks away from table edges.

subject: Science
question: What is fever, and what is the normal body temperature?
answer: Fever is a body temperature higher than normal. The normal body temperature is about 37 °C.

subject: Science
question: Give the first aid for a child with a high fever.
answer: Move the child to a cool airy place → remove heavy clothing → sponge with lukewarm water → give plenty of fluids → give the correct dose of fever medicine if available → take the child for a malaria test and treatment quickly.

subject: Science
question: What are convulsions? Give three causes.
answer: Convulsions are sudden uncontrollable jerking of the body. Causes: very high fever in a child, epilepsy, cerebral malaria or meningitis (any three).

subject: Science
question: Give any five steps of first aid for a person having convulsions, and two things you must not do.
answer: Do: stay calm and call for help; lay the person on the floor on their side away from fire, water and sharp objects; loosen tight clothing; put something soft under the head; after the fit, keep them on their side and take them to a health centre. Do not: put anything in the mouth; hold the person down or pour cold water on them.

subject: Science
question: Give the first aid for a person who has nearly drowned, and say why a weak swimmer should not jump in.
answer: Reach out to the person with a stick, rope or floating object; once out, lay them on their side so water drains; check breathing; keep them warm; if they are not breathing, give rescue breathing if trained and keep calling for help; take them to hospital. A weak swimmer should not jump in because the drowning person panics and clings, and both can drown.

subject: Science
question: Give any five ways of preventing drowning.
answer: Any five of: learn to swim; never swim alone or in flooded rivers; do not overload boats and wear life jackets; never play near wells or tanks; cover wells and tanks; watch small children near any water; do not swim after a heavy meal or in a storm.

subject: Science
question: What is fainting? Give three causes and the first aid given.
answer: Fainting is a short loss of consciousness caused by too little blood reaching the brain. Causes: standing too long in the sun, hunger, tiredness, shock or fear (any three). First aid: lay the person flat in a cool airy place, raise the legs, loosen tight clothing, allow fresh air, sponge the face, and give water when they wake.

subject: Science
question: Why is a person who has fainted made to lie down with the legs raised?
answer: Because raising the legs helps blood flow back to the brain, which is what was lacking, so the person recovers quickly.

subject: Science
question: What is a foreign body? Give the first aid for an insect in the ear and for dust in the eye.
answer: A foreign body is anything that enters the body where it does not belong. Insect in the ear: pour a little clean cooking oil or warm water to float it out, then see a health worker if it remains. Dust in the eye: do not rub; wash it out with clean water, or lift the upper eyelid over the lower one.

subject: Science
question: What should be done for a child who has swallowed paraffin, and what must never be done?
answer: The child should be taken to hospital immediately, carrying the container if possible, and kept calm and on their side. Never make the child vomit, because paraffin coming back up can enter the lungs and cause serious damage.

subject: Science
question: Give the first aid for a person choking on food.
answer: Encourage the person to cough; bend a child forward and give firm back blows between the shoulder blades; keep checking the mouth and remove anything you can see easily; call for help at once if the object does not come out.

subject: Science
question: Why should a person who has nearly drowned be taken to hospital even if they look well?
answer: Because water that entered the lungs can cause breathing problems and infection several hours later, so the person must be checked by a health worker even if they seem to have recovered.

subject: Science
question: What is sanitation?
answer: Sanitation is keeping the surroundings clean and disposing of human waste and rubbish safely so that people stay healthy.

subject: Science
question: Name any five diseases caused by poor sanitation.
answer: Any five of: cholera, typhoid, dysentery, diarrhoea, worms, bilharzia, hepatitis, jiggers.

subject: Science
question: Give the full meaning of VIP latrine.
answer: Ventilated Improved Pit latrine.

subject: Science
question: Name three special features of a VIP latrine and explain how it removes smell.
answer: Features: a vent pipe from the pit to above the roof, a fly screen at the top of the pipe, and a dark interior with an uncovered squat hole. The sun heats the vent pipe so the air inside rises and carries the smell out, while fresh air enters through the door.

subject: Science
question: How does a VIP latrine control flies?
answer: Flies in the dark pit fly towards the light at the top of the vent pipe and are trapped by the fly screen, where they die.

subject: Science
question: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of an ordinary pit latrine.
answer: Advantage: it is cheap and easy to build with local materials and needs no water. Disadvantage: it smells and attracts flies (it also fills up and must be replaced).

subject: Science
question: What is an Ecosan toilet, and what is added after each use?
answer: An Ecosan (ecological sanitation) toilet is one that separates urine from faeces and turns the waste into manure. Ash or dry soil is added after each use.

subject: Science
question: Give any three advantages of an Ecosan toilet.
answer: Any three of: it provides manure; it suits rocky, sandy, waterlogged or crowded areas; it does not pollute ground water; there is no smell when ash is used; no deep pit has to be dug.

subject: Science
question: In what kind of areas is an Ecosan toilet especially useful, and why?
answer: In rocky, sandy, waterlogged or very crowded areas, because a deep pit cannot be dug safely there and a pit would collapse or pollute the ground water.

subject: Science
question: What is a potty, and how should it be used and cleaned?
answer: A potty is a small portable container used by babies and small children who cannot use the latrine. It must be emptied into the latrine immediately, washed with clean water and soap, and dried in the sun — never emptied in the compound.

subject: Science
question: What is a water closet? Give two advantages and two disadvantages.
answer: A water closet is a flush toilet with a cistern and a water seal that carries waste to a septic tank or sewer. Advantages: it is clean and has no smell; it is comfortable and free from flies. Disadvantages: it needs plenty of piped water; it is expensive and blocks easily.

subject: Science
question: Give any six importances of using a toilet or latrine.
answer: Any six of: it prevents diseases such as cholera and worms; it keeps the compound and gardens free of human waste; it controls flies and bad smells; it protects water sources; it gives privacy and dignity; it keeps the home clean; it is required by public health law.

subject: Science
question: Explain how disease travels from faeces to the mouth, and how using a latrine breaks the path.
answer: Faeces left in the open are carried to food and the mouth by flies, fingers, food, fluids and fields — the "five Fs". Using a latrine keeps the faeces sealed in a pit so flies and feet cannot carry them, and washing hands with soap removes what is on the fingers, so the path is broken.

subject: Science
question: Give any six rules for the proper use of a latrine.
answer: Any six of: use the latrine every time; aim into the hole and keep the slab clean; cover the hole after use in an ordinary latrine; put used paper in the pit; add ash in an Ecosan toilet; flush a water closet; wash hands with soap afterwards; teach children to use the potty properly.

subject: Science
question: Give any six ways of maintaining a latrine.
answer: Any six of: sweep and scrub the floor and slab daily; use water or disinfectant; keep soap and water at the door; repair cracks, doors and roofs; keep the vent screen in good order; keep the door closed; do not throw rubbish into the pit; plant grass around it; dig a new pit when it is nearly full.

subject: Science
question: Why should rubbish and polythene never be thrown into a pit latrine?
answer: Because they do not rot, so they fill the pit quickly and shorten its life, and in a flush toilet they cause blockages.

subject: Science
question: Where should a latrine be sited in relation to a water source and the house?
answer: At least 30 metres from a water source and downhill from it, and about 6 metres from the house, downwind, on firm well-drained ground.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between a VIP latrine and an ordinary pit latrine in the way the squat hole is treated.
answer: In a VIP latrine the squat hole is left uncovered so that air can flow through the pit and up the vent pipe; in an ordinary pit latrine the hole is covered after use to keep out flies and reduce the smell.

subject: Science
question: Why should hands be washed with soap after using a latrine?
answer: Because germs from faeces remain on the fingers, and hands touch food, water and other people. Washing with soap removes those germs and prevents diseases such as diarrhoea, cholera and worms.

subject: Science
question: What should be done when a pit latrine is nearly full?
answer: It should be closed and covered with soil and a new pit dug elsewhere; the slab can be moved to the new pit, and the old site should be marked and, in time, planted with trees.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between growth and development.
answer: Growth is an increase in the size and weight of the body, while development is the change that makes the body able to do more, such as walking, talking and reproducing.

subject: Science
question: What is puberty, and at about what age does it begin in girls and in boys?
answer: Puberty is the stage at which the reproductive organs become mature and a young person becomes able to produce children. It begins at about 10–14 years in girls and 12–16 years in boys.

subject: Science
question: What is adolescence?
answer: Adolescence is the period of change between childhood and adulthood, affecting the body, the mind and the feelings.

subject: Science
question: Give any four physical changes at puberty in girls and four in boys.
answer: Girls: breasts develop; hips widen; menstruation begins; pubic and armpit hair grows (also oily skin, rapid growth). Boys: the voice deepens; the chest and shoulders broaden; wet dreams begin; facial, pubic and armpit hair grows.

subject: Science
question: Give any four social and emotional changes during adolescence.
answer: Any four of: wanting independence; strong peer influence; quick changes of mood; shyness; interest in the opposite sex; wanting privacy; new interest in appearance.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between primary and secondary sex characteristics, with two examples of each.
answer: Primary characteristics are the reproductive organs present at birth, for example the testes and the ovaries. Secondary characteristics appear at puberty, for example breasts in girls and a deep voice in boys.

subject: Science
question: Name any four parts of the male reproductive system and the work of each.
answer: Any four: testes — produce sperm cells; scrotum — holds the testes and keeps them cool; sperm duct — carries sperms; urethra — passes semen and urine out; penis — the organ through which semen and urine leave the body.

subject: Science
question: Name any four parts of the female reproductive system and the work of each.
answer: Any four: ovaries — produce egg cells; fallopian tubes — carry the egg and are where fertilisation happens; uterus — where the baby develops; cervix — the neck of the uterus; vagina — the passage to the outside.

subject: Science
question: Where are sperm cells produced, and where are egg cells produced?
answer: Sperm cells are produced in the testes; egg cells are produced in the ovaries.

subject: Science
question: What is menstruation, and about how long is the menstrual cycle?
answer: Menstruation is the monthly flow of blood and the lining of the uterus through the vagina when the egg has not been fertilised. The cycle is about 28 days.

subject: Science
question: What is fertilisation, and where does it take place?
answer: Fertilisation is the joining of a sperm cell and an egg cell. It takes place in the fallopian tube (oviduct).

subject: Science
question: Give the meaning of conception, zygote and gestation.
answer: Conception — the fertilised egg attaching to the wall of the uterus and beginning to grow; zygote — the single cell formed at fertilisation; gestation — the period the baby develops in the womb.

subject: Science
question: How long does pregnancy last, and what is the work of the placenta?
answer: Pregnancy lasts about nine months (40 weeks). The placenta supplies the baby with food and oxygen from the mother and carries away its waste.

subject: Science
question: Give any four signs of pregnancy.
answer: Any four of: the monthly periods stop; morning sickness; the breasts enlarge; the abdomen grows; tiredness; changes in appetite.

subject: Science
question: Give any six ways of caring for a pregnant mother.
answer: Any six of: attend antenatal clinic early and regularly; eat a balanced diet rich in iron; take the supplements given; sleep under a treated mosquito net; rest and avoid heavy work; avoid alcohol, smoking and self-medication; keep clean; deliver at a health centre with a trained health worker.

subject: Science
question: Give any four problems that can occur during pregnancy.
answer: Any four of: anaemia, malaria, high blood pressure, miscarriage, bleeding, excessive vomiting, obstructed labour, malnutrition, infections including HIV.

subject: Science
question: Give any five effects of teenage pregnancy and four ways of preventing it.
answer: Effects (any five): danger to the health and life of the girl and baby; obstructed labour and fistula; low birth weight; dropping out of school; poverty; stigma and rejection; unsafe abortion. Prevention (any four): stay in school; abstain from sex; avoid bad company, alcohol and drugs; refuse gifts and lifts from older people; report abuse to a trusted adult; get correct information from parents and health workers.

subject: Science
question: Give any six ways of caring for the reproductive organs.
answer: Any six of: bathe daily and wash the private parts with clean water; wear clean cotton underwear and change it daily; wipe from front to back; use and change clean sanitary materials; never insert anything into the private parts; avoid harmful traditional practices; treat itching or discharge early; abstain from sex; report anybody who touches you wrongly.

subject: Science
question: What is family planning? Give any five reasons why it is important.
answer: Family planning is deciding how many children to have and when to have them, using acceptable methods. Importance (any five): it protects the mother's health; it gives each child better care and education; it reduces infant and maternal deaths; it helps the family plan its money; it slows very rapid population growth; it allows parents to work and rest.

subject: Science
question: Name three natural and three artificial methods of family planning, and correct any two myths about family planning.
answer: Natural: abstinence, the calendar (rhythm) method, breastfeeding in the early months. Artificial: condoms, pills, injections (also implants, the loop). Myths corrected: "family planning makes a woman permanently barren" — most methods are reversible and fertility returns when they are stopped; "it is only for women" — it is the responsibility of both partners.

subject: Science
question: What is a skeleton?
answer: A skeleton is the framework of bones that supports the body and gives it shape.

subject: Science
question: Name the two main parts of the human skeleton.
answer: The axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton.

subject: Science
question: Name any four bones found in the arm and hand.
answer: Any four of: humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges.

subject: Science
question: Name the longest bone and the smallest bone in the human body.
answer: Longest — the femur; smallest — the stapes in the middle ear.

subject: Science
question: Give the three types of joints according to movement, with one example of each.
answer: Immovable — joints of the cranium; slightly movable — joints between the vertebrae; freely movable — the shoulder joint.

subject: Science
question: Name the four types of freely movable joints.
answer: Ball and socket, hinge, pivot and gliding.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between a ligament and a tendon.
answer: A ligament joins bone to bone, while a tendon joins muscle to bone.

subject: Science
question: Differentiate between voluntary and involuntary muscles.
answer: Voluntary muscles are under our control, for example the arm muscles; involuntary muscles work on their own, for example the muscles of the stomach.

subject: Science
question: Which muscles work together to bend and straighten the arm?
answer: The biceps and the triceps. The biceps contracts to bend the arm, and the triceps contracts to straighten it.

subject: Science
question: State any four functions of the muscular–skeletal system.
answer: Any four of: support, giving shape, protection of organs, movement, production of blood cells, storage of minerals, attachment of muscles.

subject: Science
question: Name the disease caused by lack of vitamin D and calcium in children and give one sign.
answer: Rickets — the child has bent (bowed) legs and soft, weak bones.

subject: Science
question: Name the four types of fractures.
answer: Simple (closed), compound (open), greenstick and comminuted.

subject: Science
question: Give the first aid you would give to a person with a fractured arm.
answer: Keep the person calm and still, do not try to push the bone back, support the arm with a splint and a sling, control any bleeding, and take the person to a health worker immediately.

subject: Science
question: Give three ways of keeping the muscular–skeletal system healthy.
answer: Any three of: eat a balanced diet rich in calcium and protein, get vitamin D from morning sunshine, exercise regularly, rest enough, avoid accidents, immunise against polio, keep correct posture.

subject: Science
question: State any three importances of correct posture.
answer: Any three of: it keeps the backbone straight, it prevents back and neck pain, it allows the lungs to work properly, it prevents deformities, it makes a person look smart.

subject: Science
question: Define electricity and name its two types.
answer: Electricity is a form of energy caused by the movement of electrons. Its two types are static electricity and current electricity.

subject: Science
question: Give any four sources of electricity used in Uganda.
answer: Any four of: dry cells, hydro-electric power, solar panels, wind, generators, geothermal, thermal (fossil fuels), biogas.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between a conductor and an insulator, with one example of each.
answer: A conductor allows electricity to pass through it, for example copper; an insulator does not, for example rubber.

subject: Science
question: Draw and label a simple electric circuit. (Cell, switch, bulb and connecting wires.)
answer: Learner's drawing. It should show a cell, connecting wires, a switch and a bulb forming a complete (closed) loop.

subject: Science
question: Give two differences between a series circuit and a parallel circuit.
answer: In a series circuit the bulbs are in one path, so if one blows all go off and the bulbs are dimmer. In a parallel circuit each bulb is on its own branch, so if one blows the others stay on and the bulbs are brighter.

subject: Science
question: What is a short circuit, and give two of its causes?
answer: A short circuit is when current finds a shorter path of very little resistance and flows without passing through the appliance. Causes: worn out or bare wires touching, water reaching the wires, overloading a socket, poor wiring.

subject: Science
question: State any four safety precautions in handling electricity.
answer: Any four of: never touch switches with wet hands; do not put metal objects in sockets; do not overload sockets; replace worn out wires; switch off the mains before repairs; keep children away from sockets; never touch fallen power lines.

subject: Science
question: Give any four uses of electricity in a home.
answer: Any four of: lighting, cooking, ironing, refrigeration, pumping water, running radios and televisions, charging phones, running computers.

subject: Science
question: Name any four magnetic materials.
answer: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between natural and artificial magnets, with one example of each.
answer: Natural magnets are found in the ground, for example lodestone; artificial magnets are made by people, for example a bar magnet.

subject: Science
question: State the law of magnetism.
answer: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

subject: Science
question: Describe how you would make a magnet by the stroking method.
answer: Place the steel bar on a table. Take one pole of a strong magnet and stroke the bar from one end to the other, always in the same direction, lifting the magnet high at the end of each stroke. Repeat many times; the bar becomes a magnet.

subject: Science
question: Give three ways in which a magnet can lose its magnetism.
answer: Any three of: heating it strongly, hammering or dropping it repeatedly, passing alternating current through it, storing it carelessly.

subject: Science
question: How are magnets properly stored?
answer: Bar magnets are stored in pairs with unlike poles facing each other and soft iron keepers placed across the ends.

subject: Science
question: Explain briefly how an electric bell works.
answer: When the switch is pressed, current flows through the electromagnet, which attracts the soft iron armature so that the hammer hits the gong. This movement breaks the circuit, the electromagnet loses its magnetism and the spring pulls the armature back, closing the circuit again. The action repeats quickly, so the bell rings continuously.

subject: Science
question: Define energy and name any four forms of energy.
answer: Energy is the ability to do work. Forms: heat, light, sound, electrical, chemical, mechanical (any four).

subject: Science
question: What is the main source of energy on earth?
answer: The sun.

subject: Science
question: Name three energy resources obtained from water.
answer: Hydro-electric power, steam energy and tidal energy.

subject: Science
question: Name the three fossil fuels.
answer: Coal, petroleum (crude oil) and natural gas.

subject: Science
question: Give two disadvantages of using fossil fuels.
answer: They pollute the air and cause global warming; they are non-renewable and will get used up. (Also: mining and drilling damage the environment.)

subject: Science
question: Name two energy resources obtained from plants.
answer: Any two of: firewood, charcoal, biofuel (ethanol or biodiesel), biogas from plant waste, crop residues such as bagasse.

subject: Science
question: What is biogas and how is it made?
answer: Biogas is a gas produced when animal dung or other organic waste rots in a digester without air. The gas is piped away and burnt for cooking and lighting.

subject: Science
question: Give three advantages of using biogas.
answer: Any three of: it is cheap and renewable; it uses waste; the slurry left over is good manure; it reduces the cutting of trees; it burns cleanly without smoke.

subject: Science
question: Give two ways in which animals provide energy.
answer: Animals give muscle energy — oxen ploughing, donkeys carrying loads — and their dung is used to make biogas.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between renewable and non-renewable energy resources.
answer: Renewable resources can be replaced or never run out, such as solar and wind; non-renewable resources get used up and cannot be replaced, such as coal and oil.

subject: Science
question: Classify these as renewable or non-renewable: solar, coal, wind, natural gas.
answer: Renewable: solar, wind. Non-renewable: coal, natural gas.

subject: Science
question: Name three hydro-electric power stations in Uganda.
answer: Any three of: Nalubaale, Kiira, Bujagali, Isimba, Karuma.

subject: Science
question: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of hydro-electric power.
answer: Advantages: it is renewable and it does not pollute the air (also cheap to run, and the dam stores water). Disadvantages: dams are very expensive to build and they may flood people's land (also affected by drought).

subject: Science
question: State any four importances of energy resources.
answer: Any four of: cooking and lighting, running industries, transport, pumping water, powering hospitals and schools, communication, creating jobs, farm work.

subject: Science
question: Suggest four ways of conserving energy in your home or school.
answer: Any four of: switch off lights and appliances not in use; use energy-saving bulbs and stoves; use solar or biogas instead of firewood; plant trees for firewood; cover pots while cooking; service vehicles regularly; walk or share transport for short journeys.

subject: Science
question: What is a simple machine? Give two ways in which machines make work easier.
answer: A simple machine is a device that makes work easier. It allows a small effort to move a big load, and it can change the direction of the force applied.

subject: Science
question: Define effort, load and fulcrum.
answer: Effort is the force applied to the machine; load is the weight or resistance the machine works against; fulcrum is the fixed point about which a lever turns.

subject: Science
question: A load of 800 N is lifted by an effort of 200 N. Find the mechanical advantage.

subject: Science
question: A machine has a mechanical advantage of 6. What effort is needed to lift a load of 540 N?
answer: Effort = 540 ÷ 6 = 90 N

subject: Science
question: State the principle of moments.
answer: Load × distance of the load from the fulcrum = effort × distance of the effort from the fulcrum.

subject: Science
question: A load of 50 N is 3 m from the fulcrum. Find the effort acting 5 m from the fulcrum on the other side.

subject: Science
question: Name the three classes of levers and give one example of each.
answer: First class — see-saw or scissors; second class — wheelbarrow; third class — fishing rod.

subject: Science
question: Name the class of lever to which a pair of pliers belongs.
answer: First class (the fulcrum is between the effort and the load).

subject: Science
question: What is an inclined plane, and give two examples?
answer: An inclined plane is a slanting surface used to raise a load. Examples: a ramp and a plank used to roll a drum onto a lorry (also staircases and zigzag hill roads).

subject: Science
question: Give two examples each of a wedge and a screw.
answer: Wedge: axe, knife (also panga, nail, chisel). Screw: bolt and nut, screw jack (also vice, corkscrew).

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between a fixed pulley and a movable pulley.
answer: A fixed pulley only changes the direction of the force, so the effort equals the load; a movable pulley reduces the effort needed, giving a mechanical advantage of about 2.

subject: Science
question: Give three examples of a wheel and axle.
answer: Any three of: steering wheel, door knob, bicycle wheel and pedals, windlass on a well, tap handle, screwdriver.

subject: Science
question: Define friction and give three examples of friction in daily life.
answer: Friction is the force that opposes movement between two surfaces in contact. Examples: brakes stopping a bicycle; shoes gripping the ground when walking; a match lighting when struck.

subject: Science
question: Give three ways of increasing friction and three ways of reducing it.
answer: Increase: make surfaces rougher; put treads on tyres and shoes; press the surfaces together more firmly. Reduce: lubricate with oil or grease; use ball bearings or rollers; polish surfaces or streamline the shape.

subject: Science
question: Give two disadvantages of friction.
answer: It wears out tyres, shoes and machine parts, and it wastes energy as heat, so machines use more fuel. (It also causes noise and overheating.)

subject: Science
question: Define excretion and give the difference between excretion and egestion.
answer: Excretion is the removal of waste products made inside the body. Egestion is the removal of undigested food (faeces), which was never part of the body's chemical processes.

subject: Science
question: Name the four excretory organs and the waste each one removes.
answer: Skin — sweat; kidneys — urine; lungs — carbon dioxide and water vapour; liver — bile pigments (and it makes urea).

subject: Science
question: Name the two main layers of the human skin.
answer: The epidermis and the dermis.

subject: Science
question: Name any four parts found in the dermis.
answer: Any four of: sweat glands, sebaceous glands, hair follicles, blood vessels, nerve endings, fatty layer.

subject: Science
question: State any four functions of the skin.
answer: Any four of: excretion of sweat, control of body temperature, protection against germs and injury, sensation, formation of vitamin D, storage of fat and water.

subject: Science
question: Name any three skin diseases and the cause of each.
answer: Any three, for example: scabies — mites; ringworm — a fungus; boils — bacteria; athlete's foot — a fungus; eczema — allergy or irritation.

subject: Science
question: Give four ways of caring for the skin.
answer: Any four of: bathe daily with soap and clean water; wear clean clothes; cut nails short; treat wounds early; eat a balanced diet and drink water; avoid sharing towels and combs; wear shoes.

subject: Science
question: Name the four parts of the urinary system in the order urine passes through them.
answer: Kidneys → ureters → urinary bladder → urethra.

subject: Science
question: Name any three parts of a kidney.
answer: Any three of: cortex, medulla, pelvis, nephrons, renal artery, renal vein.

subject: Science
question: State any three functions of the kidney.
answer: Any three of: filtering the blood, removing urea and excess salts, forming urine, controlling the amount of water in the body.

subject: Science
question: Name any three diseases or disorders of the kidney.
answer: Any three of: kidney stones, nephritis, kidney failure, bilharzia, cystitis.

subject: Science
question: How is kidney failure treated?
answer: By dialysis — cleaning the blood using a machine — or by a kidney transplant.

subject: Science
question: Which two wastes do the lungs remove?
answer: Carbon dioxide and water vapour.

subject: Science
question: Name any three diseases of the lungs and give one way of preventing lung disease.
answer: Any three of: tuberculosis, pneumonia, bronchitis, asthma, lung cancer, whooping cough. Prevention: do not smoke, keep rooms well ventilated, avoid smoke and dust, and immunise children.

subject: Science
question: Give any four good habits that keep the excretory system working well.
answer: Any four of: drink plenty of clean water; eat a balanced diet with little salt; bathe daily; exercise regularly; avoid alcohol, smoking and drug abuse; do not hold urine too long; go for medical check-ups.

subject: Science
question: Define light and give two natural and two artificial sources of light.
answer: Light is a form of energy that enables us to see. Natural: the sun, lightning (also stars, fireflies). Artificial: electric bulb, candle (also torch, lantern).

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between a luminous and a non-luminous body.
answer: A luminous body produces its own light, for example the sun; a non-luminous body does not produce light but is seen when light falls on it, for example the moon.

subject: Science
question: How does light travel? Describe one experiment that proves it.
answer: Light travels in straight lines. Take three cards with holes punched at the same height, line them up with a candle behind them; the candle is seen only when the three holes are in a straight line. When one card is moved, the light is blocked.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between transparent, translucent and opaque materials, with one example of each.
answer: Transparent lets nearly all light through (clear glass); translucent lets only some light through (frosted glass or oiled paper); opaque lets no light through (wood).

subject: Science
question: What three things are needed for a shadow to form?
answer: A source of light, an opaque object and a screen.

subject: Science
question: Give the difference between a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse.
answer: In a solar eclipse the moon comes between the sun and the earth. In a lunar eclipse the earth comes between the sun and the moon.

subject: Science
question: Describe the image formed by a pin-hole camera.
answer: It is real, inverted (upside down), laterally inverted and smaller than the object.

subject: Science
question: State the two laws of reflection.
answer: (i) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. (ii) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.

subject: Science
question: Give four characteristics of an image formed by a plane mirror.
answer: It is virtual, upright, the same size as the object, laterally inverted, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front (any four).

subject: Science
question: How does a periscope work?
answer: It has two plane mirrors fixed at 45° facing each other. Light from the object strikes the top mirror and is reflected down to the lower mirror, which reflects it into the eye of the observer.

subject: Science
question: What is refraction? Give three of its effects.
answer: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent material to another. Effects: a stick in water looks bent; a pool looks shallower than it is; a coin in water appears raised; dispersion and the rainbow (any three).

subject: Science
question: Name the seven colours of white light in order.
answer: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

subject: Science
question: Name the two types of lenses and give one use of each.
answer: Convex (converging) — used in a magnifying glass and cameras; concave (diverging) — used in spectacles for short sight.

subject: Science
question: Name any five parts of the human eye and give the work of each.
answer: Any five, for example: cornea — lets light in and starts bending it; iris — controls the size of the pupil; pupil — lets light into the eye; lens — focuses light on the retina; retina — where the image is formed; optic nerve — carries the message to the brain.

subject: Science
question: Name two eye defects and how each is corrected.
answer: Short sight is corrected with concave lenses; long sight is corrected with convex lenses.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Define the environment and name its two components.
answer: The environment is everything that surrounds a living thing. Its components are the living (biotic) and the non-living (abiotic).

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Give three ways in which animals depend on plants.
answer: Any three of: plants give animals food; plants give out oxygen; plants provide shelter and nesting materials; plants provide medicine and shade.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Give three ways in which plants depend on animals.
answer: Any three of: animals give out carbon dioxide used in photosynthesis; animal droppings and dead bodies make the soil fertile; animals pollinate flowers; animals disperse seeds; people plant and protect crops; burrowing animals aerate the soil.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Give two ways in which plants depend on other plants.
answer: Big trees give shade and shelter to smaller plants; climbing plants use others for support; fallen leaves rot into humus that feeds other plants; legumes add nitrogen to the soil (any two).

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Write down a food chain with four members.
answer: For example: grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: What is a producer? What is a decomposer?
answer: A producer is a green plant that makes its own food. A decomposer is an organism such as bacteria or fungi that rots dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Give the difference between a food chain and a food web.
answer: A food chain shows one single path of food energy, while a food web is many food chains joined together, showing that animals feed on more than one thing.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Give three ways in which plants depend on non-living things.
answer: Plants use soil for anchorage and mineral salts, water for photosynthesis and transport, air for carbon dioxide, and sunlight as the energy for photosynthesis (any three).

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Give two ways in which non-living things benefit from living things.
answer: Dead plants and animals add humus and make the soil fertile; plant roots hold the soil and prevent erosion; plants release oxygen and water vapour into the air (any two).

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Define agroforestry and name its three types.
answer: Agroforestry is the growing of trees together with crops and/or animals on the same piece of land. Types: agri-silviculture, silvo-pastoral and agro-silvo-pastoral.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: State any five importances of agroforestry.
answer: Any five of: provides firewood, timber and poles; gives shade and windbreaks; leaves make manure; roots control soil erosion; legumes add nitrogen; provides fodder, fruits and medicine; brings extra income; attracts rainfall; uses land productively.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Give three ways of caring for trees on an agroforestry farm.
answer: Any three of: watering seedlings, weeding and mulching, pruning branches, fencing against animals, applying manure, controlling pests and diseases, thinning.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Give the difference between pollarding and coppicing.
answer: Pollarding is cutting off the top branches and leaving the trunk standing, while coppicing is cutting the whole tree close to the ground so that new shoots grow from the stump.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Outline any five steps in managing a school wood project.
answer: Any five of: choose a suitable site; prepare a nursery bed and sow seeds; prepare the land and mark the spacing; transplant at the start of the rains; water and mulch; weed regularly; fence and protect from fire and animals; prune and thin; control pests; keep records; harvest properly and replant.

subject: Science
topic: Interdependence of Things in the Environment
question: Give three benefits of a school wood project.
answer: Any three of: it supplies firewood and poles for the school; it teaches learners practical skills; it earns the school money; it gives shade and beautifies the compound; it protects the soil and the environment.

subject: Science
question: Name any five common sicknesses in a home and give the cause of each.
answer: Any five, for example: malaria — a parasite carried by the mosquito; diarrhoea — germs in dirty food and water; typhoid — bacteria in contaminated food or water; worms — worm eggs from dirty hands or bare feet; cough and flu — viruses; scabies — mites.

subject: Science
question: How is malaria spread and how can it be prevented at home?
answer: Malaria is spread by the bite of an infected female anopheles mosquito. It is prevented by sleeping under a treated mosquito net, draining stagnant water, clearing bushes around the house, closing windows early, and getting tested and treated early.

subject: Science
question: Give four ways of controlling common sicknesses in a home.
answer: Any four of: keep the home clean; use a latrine and wash hands with soap; boil or treat drinking water; cover food; sleep under a treated net; immunise children; eat a balanced diet; go to a health centre early.

subject: Science
question: Name any four health and social problems facing young people today.
answer: Any four of: early pregnancy and early marriage, drug and substance abuse, HIV/AIDS and other STIs, defilement and sexual abuse, poor hygiene, child labour, peer pressure, poor nutrition.

subject: Science
question: What is anti-social behaviour? Give four examples.
answer: Anti-social behaviour is behaviour that harms other people or the community. Examples: stealing, bullying, drug abuse, vandalism, fighting, truancy, gambling (any four).

subject: Science
question: Give three effects of drug abuse on a young person.
answer: Any three of: poor health and addiction; poor performance and dropping out of school; involvement in crime and accidents; loss of money; broken relationships with family and friends.

subject: Science
question: Give three ways of preventing anti-social behaviour among young people.
answer: Any three of: guidance and counselling; using free time well in sports and clubs; choosing friends wisely and resisting peer pressure; obeying school and community rules; religious and moral teaching; reporting wrongdoing.

subject: Science
question: What should a child do if an adult tries to touch his or her private parts?
answer: The child should say NO firmly, get away from the person, and tell a trusted adult at once — a parent, teacher, health worker, religious leader or the police. The child should not keep it secret; it is never the child's fault.

subject: Science
question: What is a health survey? Give four steps followed in carrying one out.
answer: A health survey is the collecting of information about the health problems of a community so that they can be solved. Steps: choose the problem; prepare questions or a checklist; get permission from leaders; visit homes and record observations; organise the findings in tables or graphs; report to the community and health workers; suggest and take action (any four).

subject: Science
question: Give three activities, other than a survey, used to address health concerns in a community.
answer: Any three of: health education talks and radio programmes; immunisation campaigns; clean-up days; digging latrines and rubbish pits; protecting water sources; distributing mosquito nets; guidance and counselling.

subject: Science
question: Define population and census.
answer: Population is the total number of people living in a place at a particular time. A census is the official counting of all the people in a country.

subject: Science
question: Give three ways of collecting information about the population.
answer: Any three of: a national census; birth and death registers; health centre records; school registers; surveys and questionnaires; local council records.

subject: Science
question: Give four reasons why a country needs population information.
answer: Any four of: to plan for schools, hospitals, water and roads; to know the population growth rate; to plan for food and jobs; to share government services and funds fairly; to plan immunisation and other health services.

subject: Science
question: Give four problems caused by a rapidly growing population.
answer: Any four of: overcrowding and slums; pressure on schools, hospitals and water; unemployment and poverty; food shortage; land shortage and conflicts; destruction of forests and wetlands; fast spread of disease.

subject: Science
question: Name any five activities of a school health club.
answer: Any five of: cleaning the compound and latrines; checking personal hygiene; running hand-washing points; making health posters; performing drama, songs and poems; inviting health workers to give talks; growing vegetables and fruit; carrying out health surveys; keeping a first-aid box.
